sentences.text: He lengthened the tail that evening.

He did it in the kitchen with the envelope in front of him, feeling as though he were doing something slightly disloyal, and he added forty centimetres of torn sheet in bows, and he went out again the next day.
It went up thirty feet and stalled.
Thirty feet is better than eight.
Thirty feet is a real height; at thirty feet the kite was above the hedge and you had to tip your head back.
But it hung there and would not go higher and then it came down, tiredly, the way a thing comes down when it has been trying.
The crows watched.
The small one said nothing.

He lengthened it again — another sixty, which made the tail longer than the kite by a distance he found embarrassing — and this time when he got to the field the small crow made no sound at all, which he decided, after some thought, to take as approval.
The trouble that afternoon was the wind.
It was the kind that arrives in gusts and then apologises.

It would come across the field in a rush and flatten the grass in a moving line and the kite would leap, and then it would go, and there would be nothing at all for five or twelve seconds, and the kite would find itself standing on nothing.
That is not a thing you can fix with a tail.
Dai ran with it.
He ran the length of the field four times, which is what you do, and which never works as well as it does in your head.
By the fourth run the string had cut a line across his fingers and he was breathing in a way that would have embarrassed him if there had been anyone there.
There was, of course.
There were seven of them.
They came off the wire together.
Not in a scatter.
That was the thing he remembered longest — that they did not burst upward the way birds do when something startles them, all in different directions at once.
They dropped off the wire in order, from the left, at intervals, like a sentence being read.
They came out across the field low and fast and rose under the kite, and they took the line.
Seven crows, at seven points along the string, each one closing its feet on it and beating steadily.
They did not go to the kite.
They went to the *string*, spaced along it like beads, and they held the whole length of it up out of the dead air.
And they did not lift the kite.
He was certain of this afterwards and he was certain of it at the time.
They were not carrying it.
They were showing it where the wind was — holding the line at the height where the moving air was, so that the kite could find it and lean on it.
It found it.
The kite went up so fast that the string burned through his fingers before he thought to let it.

It went past the chimneys and past the church weathervane and kept going, and became a small brown shape against a very large white sky, and the crows fell away from the line one at a time and went back to the wire and sat down in a row.
Dai stood in the middle of the field with both arms shaking and the whole sky on the end of a piece of string.
